beats.narration_text: Hola — I'm Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. Chapter one left us with one sentence: the model never saw the document. That sentence turns out to hide three completely different failures, not one — and mixing them up is exactly how you reach for the wrong fix.

props.command: A model can be wrong for three different reasons — inventing an answer, citing a retired policy, or losing a fact buried in a long prompt. Which one is actually happening, and why does it matter which?
output: stale knowledge — frozen at the training cutoff
context limits — buried facts get ignored, even if they fit

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one breath: 'the model doesn't have enough information' is really three separate problems — what it invents, what it never learned had changed, and what it's handed but can't use well. Each one needs its own fix. None of them is solved by one bigger box.

show.event: Headline types in: 'One root cause. Three faces.'
Subline resolves: 'hallucination, stale knowledge, context limits — different failures, not degrees of one'
Spark line settles: 'three failures, one shared fix'

props.headline: One root cause. Three faces.
props.subline: Hallucination, stale knowledge, and context limits are different failures — not degrees of the same one.

beats.narration_text: First failure: hallucination — fluent, confident, and false, with nothing on the page to warn you. Researchers split it two ways: flatly contradicting a source, or inventing something no source can even check. Ask about a benefit the company never offered, and the model doesn't hesitate — it invents specific, plausible-sounding terms, because plausible-sounding text is exactly what it was trained to produce.

show.event: 'Hallucination' headline types in
Empty, greyed-out source shelf appears — nothing on it
A confident answer bubble writes itself anyway, no citation stamp attached
Spark line settles: 'confident ≠ correct'

props.headline: Hallucination
props.detail: Intrinsic (contradicts a source) vs. extrinsic (no source can check it) — both read equally confident (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023).

beats.narration_text: Second failure: stale knowledge. Training happens once, on a fixed snapshot — then the model deploys and stops learning while the world keeps moving. Vendor reports even state a knowledge cutoff outright. Ask about a benefit that was discontinued last year, and a model trained before the change confidently describes the old terms as current — fluently, with no flag that anything is out of date.

show.event: Timeline bar draws left to right with a cutoff marker
Label left of the marker reads 'current'; label right of it reads 'unseen'
A policy chip past the cutoff flips from 'current' to 'retired'
Model's answer bubble still reads the pre-cutoff version, unaware
Spark line settles: 'it doesn't know what it doesn't know'

props.headline: Stale Knowledge
props.subline: Frozen at the training cutoff — nothing after it exists.
props.detail: Train once, deploy, stop learning (OpenAI, 2023) — not a bug, the method.
props.sparkLine: It doesn't know what it doesn't know.

beats.narration_text: Third failure: context limits. Every request has a hard token ceiling — larger with each model generation, but never unbounded. And size alone doesn't save you: research on long-context use found accuracy highest when the answer sits at the very start or end of the input, and it drops hard when that same fact is buried in the middle — even when the whole document technically fits.

show.event: Three position markers appear: Start / Middle / End
Start and End bars rise to a high, even level
Middle bar visibly dips, a greyed fact-icon shown buried inside it
Caption settles: 'fits ≠ used'

props.caption: Qualitative shape only — the chapter states an ordering (highest at the edges, lowest in the middle), not specific accuracy numbers (Liu et al., 2024).

beats.act: worked example — the help desk hits all three
beats.narration_text: Put all three failures on one help-desk assistant. Asked about a benefit that doesn't exist, it invents one. Asked about a benefit that changed, it describes the retired version as current. Handed the entire forty-page manual and one specific question, it grabs the wrong paragraph — made worse, not safer, by cramming everything in at once. Three different failures. Same system, same day.

beats.act: why a bigger window doesn't fix any of them
beats.narration_text: So why not just make the window bigger? It doesn't stop hallucination — more blank space is still nothing to ground against. It doesn't fix stale knowledge — the training data itself never changes, no matter how much room is left over. And per the lost-in-the-middle finding, it doesn't fully fix context limits either, since a fact can technically fit and still get ignored depending on where it lands.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. Hallucination, stale knowledge, and context limits are three different failures, not three strengths of one — and 'just make the window bigger' addresses none of them by itself. The shared fix all three point toward: hand the model a small number of the right passages, chosen at the moment of the question, instead of everything at once or nothing at all. That's not a bigger box. That's choosing what goes in it.

artifactLines: Hallucination: confident, invented answers — grounding in real documents helps, but doesn't guarantee only true output (Shuster et al., 2021).
Stale knowledge: frozen at the training cutoff, with no internal flag for what's since changed (OpenAI, 2023).
Context limits: a hard token ceiling, and the 'lost in the middle' effect — a fact can fit and still get ignored depending on where it sits (Liu et al., 2024).
A bigger window fixes none of these alone — the shared answer is the right passages, chosen at question-time, not more room or none at all.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'I have a document I rely on for answers — using the three failure modes from this video, walk me through where you'd invent an answer if you'd never seen part of it, where your knowledge might already be out of date, and if I handed you the whole thing at once, where in it the important fact would most likely get lost.' Run it on something you actually rely on. Watch which of the three Claude actually names for your document — that's the whole test.
